title: Failure-Mode Analysis
subtitle: Metastable failures, retry storms, grey failures, and token-bucket retry budgets.
keyTakeaways: Distributed systems rarely fail cleanly: the most dangerous incidents are Grey Failures (degraded disk I/O, packet loss, GC pauses) and Metastable Failures where a temporary glitch triggers a self-sustaining overload loop.
Unbounded client retries without exponential backoff, jitter, and strict retry budgets turn minor transient errors into self-inflicted denial-of-service attacks.

Apply Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) to critical dependencies: evaluate failure severity, probability, and detection mechanisms, ensuring explicit fallback and load-shedding behaviors exist.

sections.heading: Metastable Failures, Retry Storms, and Grey Failures
sections.body: A metastable failure occurs when a transient trigger (such as a 10-second database freeze or network blip) pushes a system into an overload state that persists indefinitely, even long after the initial root trigger has disappeared.
bullets: The positive feedback loop of retry storms: When a service slows down, clients time out and immediately retry. The retried requests arrive on top of incoming new traffic, doubling or tripling load on an already struggling backend. The backend slows further, causing more timeouts, locking the system into a perpetual collapse.

Grey failures vs fail-stop: When a server crashes completely (fail-stop), load balancers detect the failure and reroute traffic instantly. In a grey failure, a node remains partially healthy—responding to simple `/healthz` checks in 5ms while its disk queue is saturated, taking 15 seconds to process real customer queries.

Full jitter exponential backoff: Implementing exponential backoff alone is insufficient because all clients retry at synchronized intervals, producing rhythmic waves of traffic. Adding full random jitter distributes retries evenly across time, smoothing the recovery curve.

codeSnippet.title: Full-Jitter Exponential Backoff + Token-Bucket Retry Budget

sections.heading: Severing Feedback Loops: Retry Budgets and Load Shedding
sections.body: Recovering from a metastable failure requires actively breaking the feedback loop. Simply scaling up compute often fails because new instances get crushed by the accumulated backlog the moment they join the cluster.
bullets: Token-bucket retry budgets: Restrict client-side retries to a fixed fraction of total request volume (for example, no more than 10% of total outbound requests). If error rates climb above 10%, the client drops retries immediately, preventing retry storms from compounding backend distress.

Deadline propagation: Pass request deadlines across all downstream RPC headers (e.g., `grpc-timeout`). If a request spent 800ms waiting in an upstream queue and its total client deadline is 1,000ms, downstream services discard the request immediately rather than wasting CPU on work whose client has already given up.

Priority-based load shedding: When system utilization crosses safety thresholds, drop low-priority traffic (background batch indexing, analytics tracking) at the ingress proxy to guarantee that high-priority user checkouts receive required resources.

tradeOffs.option: Aggressive Load Shedding (Drop Traffic at Gateway)
tradeOffs.pros: Protects core system stability; prevents systems from entering irreversible metastable failure loops.
tradeOffs.cons: Returns explicit errors to non-essential users or background services during traffic peaks.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Critical production backends, core transactional platforms, and shared infrastructure bottlenecks.

tradeOffs.option: Deep Queue Buffering (Buffer Backlog on Disk/Kafka)
tradeOffs.pros: Zero data loss; guarantees that every request is eventually processed once resources become available.
tradeOffs.cons: Can accumulate hours of processing lag; risks unbounded memory or disk usage during prolonged outages.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Asynchronous payroll runs, analytical event ingestion, and non-time-sensitive batch jobs.

interviewTip: Use the term "metastable failure" in senior engineering interviews: explain how a transient 10-second database stall can trigger an ongoing retry storm that keeps the system down for hours until engineers sever the feedback loop with load shedding or retry budgets.
